Alright, as the claude documentation may indicated, this is a college project.

I am trying to fix this issue:
Show a character counter next to the issue title field #2
What problem would this solve?

The issue title field enforces a maximum of 255 characters, but no counter is shown while the user is typing. Users discover the limit only when the field stops accepting input. A character counter should be displayed near the title field so users know how many characters they have remaining.
What do you propose?

As a user, I want to see a character counter next to the issue title field, so that I know how many characters I have left before reaching the limit.

I don't want you to simply give me the answer or anything like that, since I want to understand how to even navigate software like this, understand go, vue, whatever.

So, the first task is to even figure out where to make the changes, and then to figure out how to implement it for any issue field title, instead of making micro edits across multiple pages.

So lets go. I don't want to spend hours on this, but I also just don't want to answer given to me.

6	# web_src/js — page features and how they get wired up
7	
8	**Read when:** adding or changing browser behaviour on a page.
9	**Not here:** Vue components -> `frontend-vue-components.md`; styling -> `frontend-css.md`; the HTML -> `templates.md`.
10	
11	## Responsibilities
12	
13	| Directory | Owns |
14	| --- | --- |
15	| `features/` | one file per page or feature (`repo-issue.ts`, `repo-diff.ts`, `repo-code.ts`), plus `features/admin/` and `features/comp/` for shared widgets |
16	| `modules/` | cross-cutting infrastructure: `fetch.ts`, `init.ts`, `observer.ts`, `i18n.ts`, `toast.ts`, `tippy.ts`, `fomantic.ts`, `clipboard.ts`, `codeeditor/` |
17	| `utils/` | pure helpers with no DOM assumptions: `dom.ts`, `html.ts`, `url.ts`, `time.ts`, `color.ts`, `string.ts` |
18	| `markup/`, `render/` | enhancing already-rendered content (anchors, mermaid, math) |
19	| `webcomponents/` | custom elements such as `relative-time`, `overflow-menu` |
20	
21	## Key files
22	
23	| Path | What it holds |
24	| --- | --- |
25	| `web_src/js/index.ts` | the entry point: imports fomantic and `../css/index.css`, then passes every `initXxx` to `callInitFunctions` |
26	| `web_src/js/modules/init.ts` | `callInitFunctions`, `InitPerformanceTracer` |
27	| `web_src/js/modules/observer.ts` | `registerGlobalInitFunc`, `registerGlobalEventFunc`, `registerGlobalSelectorFunc`, `initGlobalSelectorObserver` |
28	| `web_src/js/modules/fetch.ts` | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` |
29	| `web_src/js/utils/dom.ts` | `showElem`, `hideElem`, `toggleElem`, `queryElems`, `createElementFromHTML` |
30	| `web_src/js/modules/i18n.ts` | `trN` — the frontend side of the locale system |
31	
32	## Conventions & invariants
33	
34	**Two ways to wire a feature, and new code should prefer the second.**
35	
36	1. *Page-load init:* export `initFoo()` from a `features/` file and add it to the array in
37	   `index.ts`. Every function in that array runs on **every** page, so it must find its elements
38	   and return immediately when they are absent.
39	2. *Declarative:* `registerGlobalInitFunc('initFoo', (el) => {...})` in the module, and
40	   `data-global-init="initFoo"` on the element in the template. For clicks,
41	   `registerGlobalEventFunc('click', 'onFoo', ...)` with `data-global-click="onFoo"`. This covers
42	   elements added to the DOM later and runs once per element (guarded by an internal
43	   `_giteaGlobalInited` flag), so re-adding a node does not re-initialise it.
44	
45	`registerGlobalSelectorFunc(selector, handler)` also exists, but `observer.ts` marks it as "less
46	efficient and less maintainable" — it is for element types already spread across many pages, not
47	for new work.
48	
49	- **Ordering rule:** every `registerGlobalInitFunc` must run *before* `initGlobalSelectorObserver`,
50	  which `index.ts` deliberately calls last. Registering after it throws.
51	- Data fetching goes through the `fetch.ts` wrappers, never a raw `fetch`.
52	- Show and hide with `.tw-hidden` plus `showElem` / `hideElem` / `toggleElem`. In Vue use
53	  `v-if`/`v-show` instead (`frontend-vue-components.md`).
54	- Use `node.getAttribute`, not `node.dataset` (camel-casing surprises), and never bind
55	  user-provided data onto a DOM node.
56	- Custom DOM events are prefixed `ce-`, declared as an exported constant next to their emitter —
57	  see `EventEditorContentChanged` in `features/comp/EditorMarkdown.ts`.
58	- TypeScript, per `docs/guidelines-frontend.md`: `import type` for type-only imports,
59	  `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore`, `!` rather than `?.`/`??` when a value always exists, and
60	  `async` only on a function that actually awaits.
61	- One feature per file or directory; ids and classes are kebab-case with 2-3 feature keywords.
62	
63	## Recipes
64	
65	**Add behaviour to an element.** Register a global init func in the owning `features/` module and
66	put `data-global-init="yourFuncName"` on the element in its template. No change to `index.ts`.
67	
68	**Add a whole-page feature.** New `features/<name>.ts` exporting `initName()`, an early return when
69	its root element is missing, then add the import and the array entry in `index.ts`.
70	
71	**Profile a slow page.** Append `?_ui_performance_trace=1` to the URL to print per-init timings.
72	`index.ts` already logs an error when total init exceeds 500ms.
73	
74	**Run one test file.** `pnpm exec vitest <path-filter>` (`testing.md`).
75	
76	## Gotchas
77	
78	- Forgetting the early return in a page-load init means that feature's cost is paid on every page
79	  in Gitea, which is what the 500ms warning is there to catch.
80	- Fomantic-UI (jQuery) is vendored and deprecated. Do not build new features on it, and do not mix
81	  it with Vue — Vue may use its CSS classes but not its JavaScript.
82	- `utils/` is for pure helpers. A function that reaches for `window` or a global selector belongs
83	  in `modules/` or `features/`.
84	
85	## Related
86	
87	- `frontend-vue-components.md` — when a feature should be a Vue app instead
88	- `templates.md` — where `data-global-init` attributes and `pageData` come from
89	- `frontend-css.md` — `tw-hidden` and the class conventions
90

Here's the map, and how I got there — the navigation method matters more than the destination.

## How I found it

Three greps, no directory spelunking:

1. `grep -rn "maxlength" templates/` — the issue says "enforces a maximum of 255 characters", and in Gitea that limit is an HTML attribute, not Go. That immediately narrows ~2000 templates to a list.
2. `grep -rn 'name="title"' templates/repo/issue/` — the form field name.
3. Then I read `.claude-students/docs/frontend-js.md`, which the repo's own `AGENTS.md` told me to read before touching `web_src/js/`.

## What's actually there

**Two** places render an issue title input:

| File | Markup |
|---|---|
| `templates/repo/issue/new_form.tmpl:9` | `<input name="title" data-global-init="autoFocusEnd" id="issue_title" required maxlength="255">` — the create page (issues *and* PRs, same template) |
| `templates/repo/issue/view_title.tmpl:31` | `<input name="title" ... maxlength="255">` — the inline "Edit" on an existing issue |

Nearby cousins with the same problem: `milestone_new.tmpl:27` (`maxlength="50"`), and `repo/issue/fields/input.tmpl` (custom issue-template fields).

## The wiring mechanism you'd use

`web_src/js/modules/observer.ts` is the important file. Gitea's modern pattern is **declarative**: you register a named function once in JS, then opt an element in from the template:

```ts
registerGlobalInitFunc('initFoo', (el) => { ... });   // web_src/js/features/*.ts
```
```html
<input data-global-init="initFoo">                     <!-- template -->
```

A `MutationObserver` (observer.ts:78) runs it for elements added later too — which matters here, because the edit-title form is `tw-hidden` until you click Edit. And observer.ts:53 guards against double-init. This is exactly the "one implementation, N templates" hook you're asking for.

**The catch you need to know about** — observer.ts:46-47:

```ts
// TODO: GLOBAL-INIT-MULTIPLE-FUNCTIONS: maybe in the future we need to extend it to support multiple functions
const initFunc = el.getAttribute('data-global-init')!;
```

One function per element, exact string match. The new-issue title input **already** uses `autoFocusEnd`. So you cannot just append yours to that input.

## The fork

That constraint is the whole design decision:

**A. Init on the wrapper, not the input.** Put `data-global-init="initInputCharCounter"` on the `<div class="field">` / `<div class="ui input">` around each title, and have the handler do `el.querySelector('input[maxlength]')`. Zero collision, zero changes to shared infra. Slightly indirect.

**B. Teach `callGlobalInitFunc` space-separated names.** Then `data-global-init="autoFocusEnd initInputCharCounter"`. The codebase literally has a TODO inviting this, and `common-page.ts:135` already queries with `~=` as if it worked. Cleanest result, but you're now editing infrastructure every page depends on.

**C. Extract a shared title-input partial** (`templates/repo/issue/title_input.tmpl`) used by both templates, so the attribute lives in one place. Composes with A or B rather than replacing it — and arguably the *real* answer to "instead of micro edits across multiple pages."

Either way you'll also need a locale key (`options/locale/locale_en-US.ini`) rather than a hardcoded English string, and a small CSS rule.

My recommendation: **B + C**. B is ~4 lines, it's the change upstream already signposted, and it leaves the counter genuinely reusable for the milestone field and anything else later. C makes the template side honest.

But A is the low-risk choice if you'd rather not touch shared infra on a first PR.

Perfect. Now I can show you the whole chain with real files. Let's go from the top.

---

# Part 1: Why your React instinct doesn't apply

In React, the browser downloads a JS bundle, and JS *builds* the DOM. `useState` works because React owns the render loop — change state, React re-renders, the number updates.

Gitea works the opposite way. It's a **server-rendered** app:

1. Browser requests `/myuser/myrepo/issues/new`
2. **Go code on the server** builds the complete HTML string
3. Browser receives finished HTML and just displays it
4. Separately, a small TypeScript bundle loads and *sprinkles* behavior onto that already-existing HTML

There is no component tree, no state, no re-render for this page. The `<input>` exists in the HTML before any JavaScript runs.

So "add a counter" splits into two unrelated jobs in two unrelated languages:

| Job | Where | Language |
|---|---|---|
| Make a `<span>` exist next to the input | template file | Go template syntax |
| Make that span's text change as you type | `web_src/js/` | TypeScript + plain DOM |

**Good news: you need neither Go nor Vue.** Go *templates* are a text-substitution syntax (closer to Jinja or Handlebars than to Go). And Vue is used elsewhere in Gitea, but not on this page at all.

---

# Part 2: Walking from URL to the actual `<input>`

Let's trace the exact page. I'll give you the four hops so you can do this yourself next time.

**Hop 1 — URL to handler.** `routers/web/web.go:1330`:

```go
m.Group("/new", func() {
    m.Combo("").Get(repo.NewIssue).
        Post(web.Bind(forms.CreateIssueForm{}), repo.NewIssuePost)
```

**Hop 2 — handler to template.** `routers/web/repo/issue_new.go:157`:

---

# Part 3: How JS attaches to server-rendered HTML

The problem Gitea has to solve: HTML arrives from the server, and JS needs to find elements and attach behavior. The naive version is `document.querySelector('#issue_title').addEventListener(...)` in a giant startup file.

Gitea's cleaner version is a **registry**. Look at `common-page.ts:122-145` — this is a complete, tiny feature attached to *your exact input*:

```ts
function autoFocusEnd(el: HTMLInputElement | HTMLTextAreaElement) {
  el.focus();
  el.setSelectionRange(el.value.length, el.value.length);
}

export function initGlobalInput() {
  registerGlobalInitFunc('autoFocusEnd', autoFocusEnd);
}
```

Read that as: *"register a function under the name `autoFocusEnd`."* Then any template, anywhere, can opt in by writing `data-global-init="autoFocusEnd"` on an element. At startup, `observer.ts` does one `querySelectorAll('[data-global-init]')`, looks up each name, and calls the function with that element.

This is the closest thing to a component in this part of the codebase: **one named function + an attribute that mounts it.** Your counter should be exactly this shape — write `initInputCharCounter` once, and every title field opts in with an attribute. That's your "instead of micro edits across multiple pages."

Two properties that matter for us:
- `observer.ts:78` wraps it in a `MutationObserver`, so elements added to the DOM *later* also get initialized. Important, because the edit-title form starts hidden.
- `observer.ts:53` sets a `_giteaGlobalInited` flag so nothing gets double-initialized.

---

The counter needs to appear in **two** places (I grepped `name="title"` across `templates/repo/issue/`):

One function per element, exact string match. Your new-issue input **already** uses `autoFocusEnd`, so you can't just append yours to it. That's the only reason my earlier options existed — every one of them was a different way around this single line.

import {getCurrentLocale} from '../utils.ts';

/** frontend `Locale.TrN`: pick the `_1` or `_n` form for `count` and interpolate `%d` */
export function trN(count: number, form1: string, formN: string, {lang = getCurrentLocale()}: {lang?: string} = {}): string {
  const form = new Intl.PluralRules(lang).select(count) === 'one' ? form1 : formN;
  return form.replace('%d', String(count));
}

# Step 1 — the text strings

**Why first:** everything downstream references these key names, so pinning them down now means no renaming later.

**Why a locale file at all:** Gitea ships in ~30 languages. A hardcoded `"characters left"` in JS can never be translated. Every user-visible string lives here, keyed by a dotted name.

**Why *two* strings:** English says "1 character left" but "2 characters left". Gitea handles this with a `_1`/`_n` pair — you saw the pattern at line 3822:

```json
"actions.runs.graph_jobs_count_1": "%d job",
"actions.runs.graph_jobs_count_n": "%d jobs",
```

The frontend helper `trN(count, form1, formN)` in `modules/i18n.ts` picks the right one and substitutes `%d` with the number. We'll use it in step 2.

I'm putting the keys at **top level** (no `repo.` prefix) rather than under `repo.issues.` — because the function we're writing works on *any* input with a `maxlength`, so the string shouldn't be issue-specific. That's what makes this reusable for the milestone field later instead of a micro-edit.

Open `options/locale/locale_en-US.json`. The file is a flat map of dotted keys, loosely grouped by topic rather than strictly alphabetical. There's a generic-UI cluster around lines 96–111.

```json

```

Watch the two things that will bite you:
- **Trailing comma** — line 108 already ends with `,` and line 109 (`"write"`) follows, so both your new lines need trailing commas too. JSON has no trailing-comma forgiveness.
- **Two-space indent**, matching its neighbours. `AGENTS.md` also says no trailing whitespace.

```text
### PR title and summary

In the PR title, describe the problem you are fixing, not how you are fixing it. \
Use the first comment as a summary of your PR. \
In the PR summary, you can describe exactly how you are fixing this problem.

PR titles must follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format, because PRs are squash-merged and the PR title becomes the resulting commit message:

```text
type(scope)!: subject
```

The scope in parentheses is optional. A `!` immediately before the colon marks a [breaking change](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#summary): either `type!:` or `type(scope)!:` (not `type!(scope):`).

Use one of these types:

- `build`: Changes affecting the build system, packaging, or external dependencies
- `ci`: Changes to CI/CD configuration files and scripts
- `chore`: Maintenance changes that do not affect production code or should not appear in the changelog
- `docs`: Documentation-only changes
- `feat`: A larger user-facing feature, improvement, or new functionality
- `enhance`: Small or trivial user-facing improvements or UX polish (for example wording changes, color adjustments, spacing or padding tweaks, placeholders, small UI behavior improvements)
- `fix`: A bug fix, UX correction, or security-related dependency update
- `perf`: Performance improvements (speed, memory, scalability)
- `refactor`: A code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature
- `revert`: Reverts a previous change
- `style`: Formatting or style-only changes that do not affect code behavior (for example lint-driven edits)
- `test`: Adding or correcting tests

Examples:

```text
fix(web): prevent avatar upload crash on empty file
feat(api): add pagination to repo hooks list
enhance(repo): improve diff toolbar spacing
ci(workflows): lint PR titles in CI
```

Keep this summary up-to-date as the PR evolves. \
If your PR changes the UI, you must add **after** screenshots in the PR summary. \
If you are not implementing a new feature, you should also post **before** screenshots for comparison.

export function createElementFromAttrs<T extends HTMLElement>(tagName: string, attrs: Record<string, any> | null, ...children: (Node | string)[]): T {
  const el = document.createElement(tagName);
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(attrs || {})) {
    if (value === undefined || value === null) continue;
    if (typeof value === 'boolean') {
      el.toggleAttribute(key, value);
    } else {
      el.setAttribute(key, String(value));
    }
  }
  for (const child of children) {
    el.append(child instanceof Node ? child : document.createTextNode(child));
  }
  return el as T;
}

export function generateElemId(prefix: string = ''): string {
  return `${prefix}${elemIdCounter++}`;
}

export type ActivePageTimerOptions = {
  once?: boolean;
  interval: () => number; // if it returns 0, the timer is stopped

# Step 2 — the TypeScript

## Where it goes and why

`web_src/js/features/common-page.ts`, right next to `autoFocusEnd`.

Two reasons, both practical:

1. **It's a generic input enhancement, not an issue feature.** Nothing about counting characters is issue-specific — it reads `maxlength` off whatever input it finds. Putting it in `repo-issue.ts` would be the "micro edit" trap; putting it beside `autoFocusEnd` says "this belongs to any input."
2. **`initGlobalInput()` is already wired into `index.ts`.** Registration must happen before `initGlobalSelectorObserver()` runs (`observer.ts:42` literally throws otherwise). Piggy-backing on an existing init function means you don't touch `index.ts` at all.

## The contract we're designing

This matters more than the code:

> Put `data-global-init="initInputCharCounter"` on an element that (a) contains one input with `maxlength`, and (b) reads sensibly when a `<span>` is appended at its end.

The container supplies the *text* via data-attributes, the input supplies the *number* via `maxlength`. The function itself knows nothing about issues. That's what makes it reusable for the milestone field later.

## Your edits

### 2a — two imports

**Line 5**, add `createElementFromAttrs` to the existing dom import:

```ts
import {addDelegatedEventListener, createElementFromAttrs, queryElems} from '../utils/dom.ts';
```

**After line 6** (the `observer.ts` import), add a new line:

```ts
import {trN} from '../modules/i18n.ts';
```

### 2b — the function

Paste this **after `applyAutoFocus`** (which ends at line 137) and **before `export function initGlobalInput()`**:

```ts
function initInputCharCounter(container: HTMLElement) {
  const input = container.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('input[maxlength], textarea[maxlength]');
  if (!input) return;

  const maxLength = Number(input.getAttribute('maxlength'));
  const textForm1 = container.getAttribute('data-char-counter-text-1')!;
  const textFormN = container.getAttribute('data-char-counter-text-n')!;

  const counter = createElementFromAttrs<HTMLElement>('span', {class: 'input-char-counter'});
  container.append(counter);

  const updateCounter = () => {
    // "maxlength" and JS string length both count UTF-16 code units, so they never disagree
    const remaining = maxLength - input.value.length;
    counter.textContent = trN(remaining, textForm1, textFormN);
    counter.classList.toggle('near-limit', remaining <= 20);
  };
  updateCounter();
  input.addEventListener('input', updateCounter);
}
```

### 2c — register it

Inside `initGlobalInput()`, add one line after the existing `registerGlobalInitFunc('autoFocusEnd', autoFocusEnd);`:

```ts
  registerGlobalInitFunc('initInputCharCounter', initInputCharCounter);
```

## Line-by-line, since several bits are Gitea-specific

**`container.querySelector(...)`; `if (!input) return;`** — the guard is the convention `frontend-js.md:37` insists on. If a template ever puts the attribute on a container with no `maxlength` input, you get nothing instead of a crash.

**`getAttribute('maxlength')`, not `input.maxLength`** — `frontend-js.md:54` says use `getAttribute`, not `dataset`, because of camel-casing surprises. Same spirit here; the attribute is the source of truth.

**The `!` on the two text lookups** — that's a TypeScript *non-null assertion*: "trust me, this isn't null." `AGENTS.md` explicitly requires `!` over `?.`/`??` when a value always exists. These always exist because the contract says the template must supply them; if one's missing you *want* the loud failure, not a silent "undefined characters left."

**`createElementFromAttrs` instead of `innerHTML`** — builds the node via `document.createElement` + `setAttribute` (`dom.ts:287`). `frontend-js.md:55` bans binding user data into DOM strings. Since the count is a number it'd be safe either way, but the habit is what keeps XSS out.

**`counter.textContent = ...`, never `innerHTML`** — same reason, and `textContent` is faster.

**`trN(remaining, textForm1, textFormN)`** — the plural helper from step 1. Picks `"%d character left"` vs `"%d characters left"` via `Intl.PluralRules` for the user's actual locale, then substitutes `%d`. This is why we made *two* keys.

**The UTF-16 comment** — this is the one genuine correctness trap. `"😀".length` is `2` in JavaScript, not 1. That looks like a bug until you know HTML's `maxlength` counts the same way, so your counter and the browser's enforcement agree exactly. `AGENTS.md` wants comments that explain *why*, not narrate code — hence that phrasing.

**No `aria-live`** — deliberate, and worth being able to defend in review. The reflex is to add `aria-live="polite"` for accessibility, but here it would make a screen reader announce on *every keystroke*, which is worse than silence. Screen reader users still get the browser's native `maxlength` enforcement. Doing this properly means announcing only at thresholds — real work, and out of scope for this issue.

Right — this is the part that doesn't transfer from React, and it's conceptual, not syntactic.

## 1. The direction of control is inverted

In React, **HTML is an output of your TypeScript.** You write JSX, React produces DOM. The compiler sees the whole path, so `<input maxLength={255}>` is type-checked end to end.

Here, **HTML is an input to your TypeScript** — and it arrives from a Go template the compiler has never heard of.

| | React | Gitea |
|---|---|---|
| Who creates the `<input>` | your TS, at runtime | Go, on the server, before JS exists |
| How TS gets a reference | it already has it | `querySelector` — goes looking |
| How TS updates the UI | set state, re-render | mutate the DOM node directly |
| Compiler sees the markup | yes | **no** |

Your TS never creates the title input. It arrives from `new_form.tmpl`, already rendered, and your job is to *find it and attach to it*.

## 2. The actual timeline on the new-issue page

Concretely, in order:

1. Go renders the full HTML. `<input name="title" maxlength="255">` exists in the document. **No JS has run.**
2. Browser parses it, starts fetching the JS bundle.
3. `index.ts:71` runs `callInitFunctions([...])`. `initGlobalInput` is in that array (line 84). Your `registerGlobalInitFunc('initInputCharCounter', ...)` fires — this **only files the function under a name in a `Record`**. Nothing has touched the DOM yet.
4. `index.ts:168` runs `initGlobalSelectorObserver(...)` — deliberately last.
5. That does one `document.querySelectorAll('[data-global-init]')` (`observer.ts:104`), and for each match reads the attribute, looks up the name, and calls your function with that element.
6. *Now* `initInputCharCounter(container)` runs, finds the input, appends a span, attaches a listener.
7. It also starts a `MutationObserver` (`observer.ts:78`). Any element added to the DOM **later** with that attribute gets initialized too.

Step 7 is why this pattern beats a plain `querySelector` at startup: the edit-title form on the issue page starts `tw-hidden` and other parts of Gitea inject markup dynamically. A startup-only query would miss those.

That ordering is also exactly why `observer.ts:42` **throws** if you register after step 4 — you'd have missed the one-time sweep.

## 3. The type boundary is real, and TypeScript cannot see across it

This is the thing to internalize:

```ts
const input = container.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('input[maxlength], textarea[maxlength]');
```

That `<HTMLInputElement>` generic is **an unchecked assertion, not a check.** `querySelector` is typed `querySelector<E extends Element>(selectors: string): E | null`. TypeScript does not parse your CSS selector, does not read `.tmpl` files, and has no idea what's in the document. You said the result is an `HTMLInputElement`, so it believes you. If the HTML changed tomorrow, TS would report nothing and you'd get a runtime `undefined`.

Same for `container.getAttribute('data-char-counter-text-1')` — typed `string | null` purely because that's `getAttribute`'s signature. TS has no idea whether the template supplies it.

So every red squiggle you *don't* see at this boundary is meaningless. The contract between `.tmpl` and `.ts` is enforced by **convention and code review only**. That's the tax for server-rendered HTML, and it's why Gitea invented the `data-global-init` registry — it at least makes the contract greppable.

## 4. So what is `!`

The **non-null assertion operator**. `expr!` means "compiler, narrow `T | null | undefined` to `T`."

It is **erased at compile time**. Zero runtime effect — the emitted JS is just `container.getAttribute('data-char-counter-text-1')`. It is not a check, not a guard, not a default.

Contrast:

```ts
const a = container.getAttribute('x')!;      // compiles to: getAttribute('x')
const b = container.getAttribute('x') ?? ''; // compiles to a real runtime ?? check
```

That's precisely why `AGENTS.md` says use `!` when a value is known to exist: `?.`/`??` emit runtime branches for conditions that can't happen, and worse, they *silently swallow* the bug. With `!`, a missing attribute gives you `"undefined characters left"` on screen — visible, and you fix the template. With `?? ''`, you get a blank counter and no clue why.

Note `maxLength` has no `!` — `Number(null)` is `0`, which TS accepts, and our selector guarantees the attribute exists anyway.

## 5. Where's the state? There isn't any

The closest thing to your `useState` instinct:

```ts
const remaining = maxLength - input.value.length;
```

There is no state variable, no store, no re-render. **The DOM node is the state.** `input.value` is the single source of truth, owned by the browser, updated by the user's keystrokes. You read it on every `input` event and write a string into another DOM node.

Which also means: no `useEffect` cleanup, no unmount. The listener lives as long as the element, the element lives until the user navigates, and navigation is a **full page reload** that destroys everything. The `_giteaGlobalInited` flag at `observer.ts:53` exists because a node removed and re-added would otherwise get a *second* counter appended.

## 6. One thing you should change while you're typing it

Now that you're looking closely — my selector matches `textarea` too, but I annotated the result as `HTMLInputElement`. That's a small lie. Both types have `.value` so it works, but make it honest:

```ts
const input = container.querySelector<HTMLInputElement | HTMLTextAreaElement>('input[maxlength], textarea[maxlength]');
```

Costs nothing, and it's the accurate claim. Go ahead and type it that way.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-12 19:02:28Z)**_

Two separate questions in there. Let me take the event first, then the discovery workflow — which is the real one.

## Why `'input'` specifically

`addEventListener('input', updateCounter)` registers `updateCounter` to run every time that event fires on that node. The event *name* is the part worth getting right:

| Event | Fires when | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `input` | value changes by **any** means — typing, paste, right-click→Paste, Ctrl+Z, drag-drop, IME composition, autofill | ✅ correct |
| `keyup` | a key is released | ❌ misses paste, undo, autofill |
| `change` | element loses focus **and** value changed | ❌ counter would sit stale until you click away |

`keyup` is the common beginner choice and it's subtly broken — paste a 300-char title and the counter doesn't move.

## How you'd know what to select

Three methods, and you should use all three in this order.

### 1. Read the template — it's the ground truth

The HTML comes from a `.tmpl` file, so the answer is always *in the repo*. You find it by grepping for something stable that appears in the rendered page:

```bash
grep -rn 'name="title"' templates/repo/issue/
```

That's exactly how I found your two files. Good things to grep for: `name="..."` (form fields), `id="..."`, a distinctive class, or a locale key you can see on screen.

The reverse trick is handy too: see a string in the browser, grep the locale JSON for it, get the key, then grep templates for that key.

### 2. Verify in the browser console

Once you have a guess, confirm it against the real page. Open devtools on the new-issue page:

```js
document.querySelectorAll('input[maxlength]')      // NodeList [input#issue_title]
document.querySelectorAll('[data-global-init]')    // everything using the registry
```

`$0` is whatever you have selected in the Elements panel, so you can poke at it directly. This is also how you check that a selector matches *exactly one* thing — if `querySelectorAll` returns 3 nodes, your `querySelector` is silently grabbing the first.

### 3. Choose a selector that's robust, not just correct

This is the part that's actually judgment. Several selectors match your input today:

```
#issue_title                              ← id, but only exists on new_form.tmpl
input[name="title"]                       ← ties you to the form field name
.field > input                            ← structural, breaks if anyone adds a div
input[maxlength], textarea[maxlength]     ← what we used
```

We picked the last one deliberately: **it selects on the thing the feature actually depends on.** The function needs a `maxlength` to count against — so match on `maxlength`. The result is that it works on the new-issue title, the edit title, the milestone field, and any input anyone adds later, with zero changes.

The general rule: prefer *semantic* selectors (attributes describing what the element is) over *structural* ones (`nth-child`, `>`, deep descendant chains). Structural selectors encode the current DOM shape, and the DOM shape is the thing most likely to change.

Note the two-level split in our design:

- `[data-global-init]` — chosen by `observer.ts`, a pure opt-in marker
- `input[maxlength]` inside the container — chosen by our function, semantic

The container never has to know what it contains, and the function never has to know which page it's on.

### The Gitea-specific convention

When you're *adding* markup rather than finding it, `frontend-js.md:61` sets the naming rule: ids and classes are kebab-case with 2-3 feature keywords. That's why the span gets `input-char-counter` and not `counter` or `charCounter` — greppable, and obviously namespaced to this feature.

You've got the mechanism right, with one correction that matters.

## It doesn't select "title" at all

Nothing in that function knows what a title is. It selects **the first `maxlength` input inside whatever container it was handed**. The word "title" appears nowhere in the TS, and that's the point.

## The container is never the page

`observer.ts:105-106`:

```ts
for (const el of document.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(selector)) {
  handler(el);
}
```

`el` is *exactly* the element carrying `data-global-init="initInputCharCounter"` — nothing wider. So scoping is decided entirely in the template, by where you put the attribute. In step 3 that's:

| Template | Container | What's inside |
|---|---|---|
| `new_form.tmpl` | `<div class="field">` | the new-issue title input |
| `view_title.tmpl` | a wrapper div we'll add | the edit-title input |

Put the attribute on two divs → exactly two counters. Put it on a milestone field later → three. The generic function never changes.

## Your hypothetical is close but the failure mode is different

If you *did* put the attribute on `<body>`, it would **not** apply to all inputs. `querySelector` is singular — first match in document order, then it stops. You'd get one counter, on whichever `maxlength` input happened to come first, appended to the end of `<body>`. Silently wrong rather than broadly applied.

`querySelectorAll` + a loop would be the "apply to all" version. We deliberately don't, because the container-per-field design gives the template precise control over *where the span lands* — and as you saw in the CSS, that placement is fiddly.

Worth naming: a container with two `maxlength` inputs would silently counter only the first. That's an accepted limitation of the contract ("one input per container"), not a bug — but it's the kind of thing a reviewer asks about.

## The footgun waiting for you in step 3

`querySelector` searches **descendants only** — never the container itself. So this looks reasonable and is broken:

```html
<input name="title" maxlength="255" data-global-init="initInputCharCounter">  <!-- ✗ -->
```

The input is the container; it has no descendants; `querySelector` returns `null`; your guard returns early; nothing happens, no error. It has to be a wrapper:

```html
<div class="field" data-global-init="initInputCharCounter">   <!-- ✓ -->
  <input name="title" maxlength="255">
</div>
```

Which is precisely why approach A works and why the guard exists. Silent-return is the right behavior here (a stray attribute shouldn't break the page), but it does mean *"I added the attribute and nothing happened"* is a debugging session. First thing to check is always: is the attribute on a wrapper?

Two one-character-ish mistakes, zero compile-time signal. That's the tax for the template↔TS boundary, and it's why "it type-checks" means much less here than in a React app.

`getAttribute('maxLength')` — this genuinely *works* (the DOM spec lowercases attribute names for HTML elements), so it's not a bug. The git convention is that a subject completes the sentence *"If applied, this commit will ___"*. Your `chore(locale): Added character strings…` from step 1 went the other way, and so does this one.

Don't fix the step-1 commit though — `AGENTS.md` says never amend or force-push, and the whole branch gets squash-merged anyway, so it costs nothing.

**2. Scope is a domain, not a directory.** Every scope in the history is a subsystem: `actions`, `util`, `web`, `ui`, `api`, `pull`, `lfs`, `locale`, `turnstile`. None is a file path. `js/features` reads as "where I edited," but scope is meant to say "what area this affects." `ui` is the fit here.

**3. `feat` overstates it.** CONTRIBUTING.md:184 defines `feat` as "a larger user-facing feature." This commit adds a function that literally nothing calls yet — no template references it, nothing renders. And the eventual PR title will be `enhance` (line 185: "small UI behavior improvements"), so `feat` here is also inconsistent with where this is heading.

Because of the squash, branch-commit types are low-stakes — but matching the PR keeps it tidy.

## Suggested

```
enhance(ui): add reusable character counter for inputs with maxlength

Assisted-by: Claude Code:claude-opus-5
```

"reusable … for inputs with maxlength" says the thing that matters — it's generic, not issue-specific — where `initInputCharCounter` just names an internal symbol a reader can grep for anyway.

```bash
git add web_src/js/features/common-page.ts
git commit -m "enhance(ui): add reusable character counter for inputs with maxlength" -m "Assisted-by: Claude Code:claude-opus-5"
```

One optional nit: `AGENTS.md` says "prefer same-line" comments, so that contract note could be `//` rather than a `/** */` block. The file has both styles, so it's genuinely fine as-is.

Ready for step 3, the templates. That's where the Go template syntax comes in, plus the flex-layout wrinkle on the edit-title page I flagged earlier.

# Step 3 — the templates

## 3a — first, rename the attributes (my mistake)

I named them `data-char-counter-text-1`. The repo has a clear convention I should have matched: **dozens** of `data-locale-*` attributes for translated strings handed to JS, e.g. `view_component.tmpl:51`:

```html
data-locale-graph-jobs-count-1="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "actions.runs.graph_jobs_count_1"}}"
```

The prefix tells a reader "this is a translated string, don't hardcode it." Worth matching — a reviewer would flag it.

In `common-page.ts`, change those two lines to:

```ts
  const textForm1 = container.getAttribute('data-locale-chars-left-1')!;
  const textFormN = container.getAttribute('data-locale-chars-left-n')!;
```

## 3b — `templates/repo/issue/new_form.tmpl`

Line 8 is currently `<div class="field">`. Replace it with:

```html
					<div class="field" data-global-init="initInputCharCounter"
							data-locale-chars-left-1="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_1"}}"
							data-locale-chars-left-n="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_n"}}"
					>
```

**Tabs, not spaces** — the `.tmpl` files are tab-indented, and `.editorconfig` will fight you otherwise. `<div class="field">` sits at 5 tabs.

No new markup at all. `.field` already wraps the input, so it satisfies the contract as-is.

One caveat worth knowing: on the **compare/PR** page, `.field` also contains the `title_wip_desc` hint (line 13), so the counter appends *after* that hint rather than directly under the input. Acceptable, and avoiding it would mean adding a wrapper div for a cosmetic gain.

## 3c — `templates/repo/issue/view_title.tmpl`

This one needs a wrapper, because of the CSS I found earlier:

```css
.repository.view.issue .issue-title { display: flex; gap: 0.5em; }
.repository.view.issue .issue-title .ui.input { width: 100%; height: 35px; }
```

`.ui.input` is a **fixed 35px-tall flex child**. Appending a span inside it would cram the counter into the input box. So we add one wrapper that owns the vertical stacking.

Replace lines 29-31:

```html
		<div class="ui input tw-flex-1">
			<input name="title" value="{{.Issue.Title}}" data-old-title="{{.Issue.Title}}" maxlength="255" autocomplete="off">
		</div>
```

with:

```html
		<div class="tw-flex-1" data-global-init="initInputCharCounter"
				data-locale-chars-left-1="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_1"}}"
				data-locale-chars-left-n="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_n"}}"
		>
			<div class="ui input">
				<input name="title" value="{{.Issue.Title}}" data-old-title="{{.Issue.Title}}" maxlength="255" autocomplete="off">
			</div>
		</div>
```

Note `tw-flex-1` **moves** from `.ui.input` to the new wrapper — the wrapper is now the flex child that needs to expand. `.ui.input` keeps `width: 100%` from the existing CSS rule, so it still fills the wrapper. No CSS change needed here.

## The Go template syntax you're using

```
{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_1"}}
```

- `ctx` — the request context, available in every template
- `.Locale.Tr` — "translate," reading `locale_en-US.json` for the user's language
- `"chars_left_1"` — your key from step 1, no prefix because we made it top-level

The nested quotes (`data-x="{{... "key"}}"`) look wrong but are correct — Go parses `{{...}}` before the HTML attribute is assembled. And `Tr` HTML-escapes its output, so a translation containing `&` or `<` can't break your markup.

## One edge case you should know about

`repo-issue.ts:388` does this when you click Edit on a blank title:

```ts
issueTitleInput.value = oldTitle;
```

**Setting `.value` in JS does not fire an `input` event.** That's a DOM rule, not a Gitea quirk — `input` means *user*-initiated change. So in that narrow path (blank the title → save → click Edit again) the counter would show a stale number until the next keystroke.

It's obscure enough that I'd leave it and mention it in the PR rather than reach into another file. Flagging it because it's the kind of coupling that bites generic widgets, and you'd rather hear it from me than from a reviewer.

Make those three edits and I'll run `make lint-js` and check the templates render.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-12 19:28:45Z)**_

Two findings, and the second one matters more than the highlighting.

## Why you couldn't find the setting

You have **no Go-template extension installed**. Your extensions are:

```
anthropic.claude-code, catppuccin (x2), dbaeumer.vscode-eslint,
esbenp.prettier-vscode, pixl-garden.bongocat,
streetsidesoftware.code-spell-checker, supabase.vscode-supabase-extension
```

So "put the extension format in the extension's settings" had nothing to configure — that instruction was from some extension's README, not this repo. I grepped; Gitea documents `.tmpl` indentation (`.editorconfig:12`) but never editor highlighting.

## The zero-install fix

`.tmpl` is HTML with `{{...}}` sprinkled in. Tell VS Code to treat it as HTML and you get 90% of the benefit — tags, attributes and strings all colored, `{{...}}` just renders as plain text.

If you want real `{{...}}` highlighting, install a Go template extension, then check its language ID via **Ctrl+Shift+P → "Change Language Mode"** and use that ID instead of `"html"` below. I won't guess an ID at you — they differ per extension.

## The part that actually matters

You have `"editor.formatOnSave": true` and **Prettier** installed. This repo uses three different linters, none of them Prettier:

```
make lint-js    → eslint (@stylistic rules)
make lint-css   → stylelint
make lint-json  → its own JSON formatting check
```

Prettier will fight all three. There's already evidence it did: remember the eslint error on your import?

```
10:9  error  There should be no space after '{'   @stylistic/object-curly-spacing
```

You typed `import { trN }`. `{ trN }` with inner spaces is **Prettier's default**; Gitea's eslint wants `{trN}`. That wasn't a typo — your editor did it on save.

And this gets worse the moment you associate `.tmpl` with HTML: Prettier would then format `.tmpl` files on save, reflowing `{{if}}` blocks and converting the required tabs to spaces. It would mangle templates.

## What to create

`.vscode/settings.json` **in the repo root**. It's in `.gitignore:22`, so it stays personal and won't show up in your PR — but it's scoped to this project instead of polluting your global settings.

```json
{
  "files.associations": {
    "*.tmpl": "html"
  },
  "[html]": {
    "editor.formatOnSave": false
  },
  "[typescript]": {
    "editor.formatOnSave": false
  },
  "[css]": {
    "editor.formatOnSave": false
  },
  "[json]": {
    "editor.formatOnSave": false
  },
  "editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
    "source.fixAll.eslint": "explicit"
  }
}
```

Line by line:

- **`files.associations`** — the highlighting fix.
- **The four `[lang]` blocks** — disable Prettier on save for exactly the file types this repo lints itself. Your global `formatOnSave` stays on everywhere else.
- **`codeActionsOnSave` with eslint** — you don't lose auto-formatting, you get the *right* one. This runs `eslint --fix` on save, which is the same thing `make lint-js-fix` does. Your editor and CI now agree instead of undoing each other.

You already have `dbaeumer.vscode-eslint` installed, so that last line works immediately.

Create that, then go ahead with the three step-3 edits — the attribute rename in `common-page.ts`, and the two templates.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-12 19:47:49Z)**_

`make lint-templates` needs `uv` (Python), which isn't installed — so no automated catch. I found it by reading. Everything else is correct: the TS rename, the wrapper nesting, and moving `tw-flex-1` to the wrapper are all exactly right.

## The bug — same in both files

```html
data-locale-chars-left-1="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_1"}}  data-locale-chars-left-n="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_n"}}""
```

You collapsed my two lines into one and lost a quote. Trace how the browser parses it, remembering **Go runs first** and substitutes the translations before HTML parsing ever happens:

1. `data-locale-chars-left-1="` opens the value
2. Go substitutes → `%d character left`
3. HTML keeps consuming: `  data-locale-chars-left-n=` is still *inside* the attribute value
4. The next `"` **closes attribute 1**

So you end up with:

```
data-locale-chars-left-1 = "%d character left  data-locale-chars-left-n="
```

and **`data-locale-chars-left-n` never exists.** The trailing `""` is stray.

## What that does at runtime

Worse than a missing counter. `textFormN` is `null`, and `trN` does:

```ts
const form = ... === 'one' ? form1 : formN;
return form.replace('%d', String(count));
```

`updateCounter()` runs immediately at init with `remaining = 255`. `Intl.PluralRules.select(255)` returns `'other'` → `form` is `null` → `null.replace(...)` → **TypeError**, thrown inside the startup sweep in `callGlobalInitFunc`. That can take out other page initialization with it, not just your feature.

This is also the flip side of that `!` conversation: `!` told TypeScript "trust me, never null," and the template quietly made it null. The assertion moved the failure to runtime — which is what you want (loud, traceable) versus `?? ''` (silent blank counter forever).

## The fix — keep them on separate lines

`new_form.tmpl`, line 8:

```html
					<div class="field" data-global-init="initInputCharCounter"
							data-locale-chars-left-1="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_1"}}"
							data-locale-chars-left-n="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_n"}}"
					>
```

`view_title.tmpl`, line 30:

```html
		<div class="tw-flex-1" data-global-init="initInputCharCounter"
				data-locale-chars-left-1="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_1"}}"
				data-locale-chars-left-n="{{ctx.Locale.Tr "chars_left_n"}}"
		>
```

One attribute per line isn't just style here — nested quotes like `data-x="{{... "key"}}"` are genuinely hard to eyeball, and one per line makes an unbalanced quote obvious. Your new `.tmpl` → HTML association should now color these too, so a broken quote will show up as the wrong color for the rest of the line.

Two small notes while you're in there:

- Optional: `sudo zypper install uv` (you're on openSUSE) would let `make lint-templates` run and catch this class of thing automatically.
- Your commit subject has `maxlenght` — don't amend it (`AGENTS.md` forbids that, and the branch gets squashed anyway), just worth knowing it's there.

Fix both lines and I'll re-check, then we do the CSS.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-12 19:52:15Z)**_

Yes on both counts.

**It is a Python package manager — but it's written in Rust.** That's what makes the name confusing. From the package description:

> uv is a Python package installer and resolver, written in Rust. Designed as a drop-in replacement for common pip and pip-tools workflows.

So it *manages* Python; it isn't *written in* Python. It's from Astral, the same people as `ruff`.

**And you're right about the package name.** openSUSE's convention prefixes anything shipping a module for a specific interpreter with `python3XX-`, so the source package `python-uv` builds `python313-uv` and `python314-uv`. But note the Provides list:

```
Provides : uv = 0.12.12
```

So `sudo zypper install uv` *would* resolve — it just leaves zypper to pick between the 3.13 and 3.14 flavors. Being explicit is better:

```bash
sudo zypper install python313-uv
which uv    # confirm the unversioned binary landed
```

## What Gitea actually uses it for

`Makefile:598`:

```make
.venv: uv.lock
	uv sync
```

`uv sync` reads `pyproject.toml` and builds a local `.venv` with three dev tools:

```toml
dev = ["djlint==1.40.1", "yamllint==1.38.0", "zizmor==1.26.1"]

[tool.djlint]
profile = "golang"
```

**`djlint` with `profile="golang"` is your template linter** — it parses HTML that contains `{{...}}`. That's precisely the tool that would have flagged the unbalanced quote I caught by hand. Worth the 52 MB for this project specifically.

After installing, `make lint-templates` should work and you can use it as a check on step 3 instead of relying on me reading the diff.

Still outstanding: the two template lines, one attribute per line.

5	
6	# web_src/css — styling conventions
7	
8	**Read when:** adding or changing styles, or deciding between a Tailwind utility and a new class.
9	**Not here:** the markup -> `templates.md`; show/hide behaviour -> `frontend-js.md`.
10	
11	## Responsibilities
12	
13	All stylesheets, aggregated by `index.css`, which imports the module replacements, the helpers and
14	then the per-area files. The build is vite + Tailwind, configured in `tailwind.config.ts`.
15	
16	| Directory | Owns |
17	| --- | --- |
18	| `modules/` | replacements for Fomantic-UI's components (`button.css`, `dropdown.css`, `form.css`, `modal.css`, ...) |
19	| `shared/` | styles shared across several areas |
20	| `features/` | per-feature styles (`heatmap.css`, `imagediff.css`, `projects.css`, `gitgraph.css`) |
21	| `repo/`, `markup/`, `editor/`, `themes/` | repo sub-areas, rendered markup, the editors, and the theme variables |
22	| top-level files | one per page area: `repo.css`, `admin.css`, `user.css`, `org.css`, `explore.css`, `dashboard.css`, `review.css`, `actions.css`, `install.css` |
23	
24	## Key files
25	
26	| Path | What it holds |
27	| --- | --- |
28	| `web_src/css/index.css` | the import list — a new stylesheet must be added here |
29	| `web_src/css/helpers.css` | the `gt-` and `g-` custom helpers |
30	| `web_src/css/base.css` | base element styles and shared variables |
31	| `web_src/css/themes/` | per-theme variable definitions |
32	| `tailwind.config.ts` | the `tw-` prefix, the content globs and the blocklist |
33	
34	## Conventions & invariants
35	
36	- **Tailwind utilities are prefixed `tw-`** (set in `tailwind.config.ts`), so `tw-hidden`,
37	  `tw-flex`. An unprefixed Tailwind class does nothing.
38	- Prefer the `flex-*` layout helpers over per-child `tw-ml-*` / `tw-mr-*` margins (`AGENTS.md`).
39	  Fall back to `tw-*` utilities where specificity forces `!important`.
40	- Gitea's own helpers live in `helpers.css`: `gt-` for general helpers, `g-` for framework-level
41	  ones. Use them **only where Tailwind has no utility** — do not add a `gt-` class that duplicates
42	  a `tw-` one.
43	- **Never edit a framework class to restyle something.** Create a new class name and apply it
44	  alongside (`docs/guidelines-frontend.md`).
45	- Avoid `!important`; where it is unavoidable, leave a comment saying why. The existing `gt-`
46	  helpers use it deliberately, which is why they win over framework rules.
47	- Class and id names are kebab-case with two or three feature keywords, prefixed to avoid
48	  collisions between frameworks.
49	- In a template, write the class attribute as one readable unit rather than concatenating:
50	
51	  ```html
52	  <div class="flex-text-inline {{if .IsFoo}}tw-hidden{{end}}"></div>
53	  ```
54	
55	- `tw-hidden` is also the show/hide mechanism used by `showElem`/`hideElem` in
56	  `frontend-js.md` — do not reuse it as a generic styling class.
57	
58	## Recipes
59	
60	**Style a new feature.** Add `web_src/css/features/<name>.css`, import it from `index.css`, and use
61	a `.<feature>-` class prefix so the names cannot collide.
62	
63	**Restyle a Fomantic component.** Look in `web_src/css/modules/` first — many components are
64	already replaced there, and the replacement is the file to change.
65	
66	**Add a theme-aware colour.** Use the variables from `themes/`, never a literal colour, or the
67	other themes break.
68	
69	## Gotchas
70	
71	- Forgetting the `@import` in `index.css` means your file compiles to nothing, with no error.
72	- The Tailwind `content` globs in `tailwind.config.ts` decide which classes survive the build. A
73	  class assembled dynamically in JavaScript will be purged — write the full class name literally.
74	- `tailwind.config.ts` has a `blocklist`; a utility that mysteriously does not exist may be listed
75	  there on purpose.
76	- `web_src/css/modules/` is Gitea's *replacement* for Fomantic, not Fomantic itself — the vendored
77	  original is under `web_src/fomantic/`.
78	
79	## Related
80	
81	- `templates.md` — where these classes are written
82	- `frontend-js.md` — `tw-hidden` and the DOM helpers
83

---

# Step 4 — the CSS

## Where, per the repo's own doc

`frontend-css.md:18` says `modules/` is *"replacements for Fomantic-UI's components"* — so my earlier instinct to use `input.css` was wrong, and that file says so itself in its header comment. Line 60 gives the right recipe:

> **Style a new feature.** Add `web_src/css/features/<name>.css`, import it from `index.css`, and use a `.<feature>-` class prefix so the names cannot collide.

## 4a — create `web_src/css/features/char-counter.css`

```css
.input-char-counter {
  display: block;
  margin-top: 4px;
  text-align: end;
  font-size: 12px;
  color: var(--color-text-light-2);
}

.input-char-counter.near-limit {
  color: var(--color-warning-text);
}
```

Note this file is **2-space indented** — CSS, unlike `.tmpl` and `.go`, isn't in the tab list in `.editorconfig`.

Four things worth understanding:

**`display: block`** — `createElementFromAttrs('span', ...)` makes a `<span>`, which is inline by default and would sit *beside* the input. Block puts it on its own line underneath.

**`text-align: end`, not `right`** — a logical property. Gitea supports RTL languages (that's what `attachInputDirAuto` at `common-page.ts:105` is doing with `dir="auto"`). `end` means "right in LTR, left in RTL"; `right` would strand the counter on the wrong side for Arabic or Hebrew users.

**Theme variables, never literals** — `frontend-css.md:66`. `--color-text-light-2` (`#5b6167` in the light theme) and `--color-warning-text` (`#9a6700`) are both defined per-theme in `themes/`. A hardcoded hex would look wrong in dark mode and in the other ~10 themes.

**The compound selector `.input-char-counter.near-limit`** — requires *both* classes. `near-limit` alone is a generic name that could collide someday; requiring both means our rule can never accidentally style someone else's element. I grepped — nothing else in the codebase uses `near-limit` today.

## 4b — register it in `index.css`

Add after line 50 (`@import "./features/captcha.css";`):

```css
@import "./features/char-counter.css";
```

**This is the step that's easy to skip and painful to debug.** `frontend-css.md:71`:

> Forgetting the `@import` in `index.css` means your file compiles to nothing, with no error.

No warning, no build failure — your CSS just silently doesn't exist, and you'd be hunting through JS wondering why the span has no styling.

Once both are done, run `make lint-css` and I'll check it. Then step 5: actually running the app, which you need anyway for the before/after screenshots CONTRIBUTING requires.

Checked both ways, and the evidence says yes — though not for the reason you'd guess.

**Size isn't the argument.** `features/cropper.css` is **6 lines**. Your 8-line file would be the *second*-smallest, not an outlier. This codebase already treats "small but distinct" as worth a file.

```
  6  cropper.css
 33  captcha.css
 59  dropzone.css
 60  heatmap.css
```

**The real argument is what `form.css` is.** I grepped it for plain single-class selectors — **zero**. Every rule in its 473 lines is `.ui.form`-something. It's a strict Fomantic replacement, and dropping `.input-char-counter` in there makes it no longer that. `frontend-css.md:43` is pointed about this:

> Never edit a framework class to restyle something. Create a new class name and apply it alongside.

So it's less "this is generic enough to deserve a file" and more "there's no existing file it belongs in without muddying that file's contract." `base.css` is base element styles, `helpers.css` is `gt-`/`g-` utilities, `modules/` is Fomantic. `features/` is the only honest home.

You're right that it's ceremony — two files touched for eight lines. But it's the cheap kind: the import is one line, and it means the next person grepping `input-char-counter` finds one file instead of line 300-something of a 473-line Fomantic file.

Go ahead with 4a and 4b as written, then `make lint-css`.

## One small thing first

`char-counter.css` has **no final newline** — the file ends at `}` (I checked the last byte: `0x7d`). `.editorconfig:9` requires `insert_final_newline = true` for all files. Stylelint doesn't check this, so nothing caught it.

```bash

```

**Why it happened, and how to stop it recurring:** you don't have the EditorConfig extension installed, so VS Code isn't reading `.editorconfig` at all. That's also what let the trailing whitespace through back in step 2. Install it:

```bash
code --install-extension EditorConfig.EditorConfig
```

That makes VS Code honor the repo's own rules automatically — final newlines, trailing whitespace, **and** the `indent_style = tab` rule for `.go`/`.tmpl`/`.html` at line 12. Better than hand-adding settings, because it picks up per-filetype rules you'd otherwise have to replicate.

Found the house style. Two files agree on how Gitea does field hint text:

```css
/* form.css:414 — the standard hint under a field */
.form .help {
  color: var(--color-secondary-dark-5);
  margin-top: 0.25em;
  display: inline-block;
}
```

Note what it *doesn't* do: no right-alignment, no `display: block`. Hints sit at the **start** of the field, directly under where the text begins. That's why yours feels unmoored — it's the only hint in Gitea that floats right.

## Replace `char-counter.css` with

```css
.input-char-counter {
  display: inline-block;
  margin-top: 0.25em;
  font-size: 12px;
  color: var(--color-secondary-dark-5);
}

.input-char-counter.near-limit {
  color: var(--color-warning-text);
}
```

Four changes, each matching something that already exists:

| Was | Now | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `text-align: end` | *removed* | the actual culprit — right-aligning stranded it between the input edge and the Cancel button |
| `display: block` | `inline-block` | matches `.form .help`; the span still wraps to its own line because `.ui.input` is `width: 100%` |
| `margin-top: 4px` | `0.25em` | house value, and `em` scales with font size instead of being a fixed 4px |
| `--color-text-light-2` | `--color-secondary-dark-5` | the variable Gitea actually uses for hint text (`#7a8188` light / `#7d828c` dark). Mine was the color used for *metadata* like the `#123` issue number |

I kept `font-size: 12px` — `.form .help` inherits its size, but the edit-title form sets `font-size: 1.5em` on the input, so inheriting there would give you a comically large counter. Worth the deviation.

Reload and it should read as a normal Gitea field hint rather than a floating label.

But if `247 characters left` on a nearly-empty field still feels noisy once it's left-aligned, hiding it until ~50 remaining is a two-line change in `updateCounter`. See how it looks first.

## 1. Where the classes are used — nowhere in any template

That grep is the complete answer. Four hits, zero templates:

```
common-page.ts:151   createElementFromAttrs('span', {class: 'input-char-counter'})
common-page.ts:158   counter.classList.toggle('near-limit', remaining <= 20)
char-counter.css:1   .input-char-counter {
char-counter.css:8   .input-char-counter.near-limit {
```

**The `<span>` doesn't exist in any `.tmpl` — JS creates it at runtime.** The template only supplies the *container* (`data-global-init` + the two locale attributes); everything inside is built by `initInputCharCounter`.

Practical consequence: "View Source" on the page will never show it, because view-source shows what the Go server sent. You'll only find it in devtools' **Elements** panel, which shows the live DOM after JS has run. Worth internalizing — it's a standing source of confusion in server-rendered apps with JS enhancement.

This is also why `frontend-css.md:73` warns that a class *assembled* in JS (e.g. `` `near-${x}` ``) gets purged by Tailwind. Ours are written as literal strings and are hand-written CSS rather than Tailwind utilities, so they're safe — but it's the same trap.

## 2. Yes, there should be a danger state

Good catch. `--color-error-text` is the semantic one (`#d1242f` light, `#f85149` dark) — better than raw `--color-red`, which is the palette primitive.

**`char-counter.css`** — add a third rule:

```css
.input-char-counter.at-limit {
  color: var(--color-error-text);
}
```

**`common-page.ts:158`** — replace that line with two:

```ts
    counter.classList.toggle('near-limit', remaining <= 20 && remaining > 0);
    counter.classList.toggle('at-limit', remaining <= 0);
```

Two deliberate details:

**Mutually exclusive in JS, not by CSS order.** Both conditions would otherwise be true at 0 remaining, and which color won would depend on which rule sits lower in the file — a trap for whoever reorders that file later. Making them exclusive means the CSS rules are order-independent.

**`<= 0`, not `=== 0`.** `maxlength` stops you *typing* past 255, but it does **not** truncate a value the server already rendered. Look at `new_form.tmpl:11`:

```
value="{{if .TitleQuery}}{{.TitleQuery}}{{else if .IssueTemplateTitle}}{{.IssueTemplateTitle}}{{else}}{{.title}}{{end}}"
```

A `?title=` URL query or an issue template title longer than 255 chars lands in the field intact. `remaining` goes negative, the form will fail server-side validation, and showing danger is exactly right. It'll read `-3 characters left`, which is odd-looking but honest — and it's a state the user genuinely needs to see.

Make those two edits, `make lint-css` and `make lint-js`, and it's done bar the test and the PR.

# Maintenance rules

Five people maintain one shared set of docs. These rules exist so the set stays *one* set. Read
them before editing anything in `.claude-students/`. Rules marked **[checked]** are enforced by
`./.claude-students/check.sh`.

## Scope discipline

1. **Upstream wins.** `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/guidelines-*.md` are authoritative.
   Docs here summarise them and link to them; they never restate a rule differently and never
   contradict one. A contradiction is a bug in this folder, not in the project.
2. **One fact, one home.** Every fact lives in exactly one doc — the one whose `scope:` owns that
   path. Everywhere else, link to it. Duplicated facts are how five maintainers end up with five
   different answers.
3. **Durability test.** Record a fact only if it (a) took more than one discovery step to find and
   (b) will still be true after the next upstream merge. A one-off workaround, a sprint detail or
   anything about your own task fails this test — that belongs in `ai-logs/`.
4. **No process notes.** No TODOs, no open questions, no first person, no student names, no dates
   other than `verified-at`. This is a map of the code, not a journal.

## Form

5. **Template only [checked].** Use the `## ` headings from `_TEMPLATE.md`, all of them, in that
   order, with nothing added. If a section has nothing to say, write one line saying so.
6. **120-line cap [checked].** Going over means the scope is too broad. Split the doc, and add the
   new `INDEX.md` row in the same commit. `INDEX.md` itself is capped at 60 lines.
7. **Cite or delete [checked, partially].** Every claim names a repo path. A claim with no path is
   unverifiable by the next reader — delete it.
8. **Symbols, not line numbers [checked].** Write `models/db/context.go` → `WithTx`, never
   `models/db/context.go:143`. Line numbers rot at the next upstream merge and a stale number is
   worse than no number. Code fences stay at 10 lines or fewer — point at the file instead of
   copying it.
9. **Repo-relative paths [checked].** `models/db/context.go`, never `/home/you/gitea/models/...`.
10. **Whitespace [checked].** No trailing whitespace, LF endings, final newline — same as the rest
    of the repo (`.editorconfig`).

## Change control

11. **One universal set.** These docs live on `main` and nowhere else. Never keep a personal copy,
    a per-student folder, or a long-lived branch of them.
12. **Changes land by PR**, titled `docs(context): <subject>` per `AGENTS.md` Conventional Commits,
    with an `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer and no `Co-Authored-By` or
    `Signed-off-by`.
13. **Fix in place.** If you discover while working that a doc is wrong or incomplete, correct it
    in the *same* PR as your code change and update `verified-at` to the commit you checked
    against. Leaving a doc stale for someone else to hit is the exact failure this folder exists to
    prevent. This rule applies to AI sessions too.
14. **New docs need three things in one commit [checked]:** the file, its `INDEX.md` row, and a
    `scope:` that does not overlap any existing doc's. If the scope overlaps, you wanted to edit
    that doc, not add one.
15. **`./.claude-students/check.sh` passes before you push [checked].** It is dependency-free and
    finishes in under a second.

## The guide layer (rules 16-22)

`guide/` holds a plain-English page for each reference page in `docs/`, same filename. It exists so
a person new to Go and to this codebase can get oriented. It is **derived**, not independent.

16. Every guide carries `source:`, `source-hash:` and `verified-at:` in its frontmatter **[checked]**.
17. A guide's `source:` names a real `docs/*.md` with the **same filename** **[checked]**.
18. `source-hash:` is the first 16 characters of `sha256sum docs/<name>.md`. If the reference page
    changes and the guide is not regenerated, `check.sh` reports **drift** **[checked]**. Regenerating
    means: reread the reference page, rewrite the guide, update the hash and `verified-at`.
19. Guide headings match `guide/_TEMPLATE.md` exactly and in order **[checked]**.
20. Guides are capped at **200 lines**, code fences at **30** **[checked]** — teaching needs more room
    than reference does.
21. **A guide adds explanation, vocabulary and worked steps. It adds no new facts.** Every repo path
    a guide cites must also be cited by its source page **[checked]**. If you need a fact the
    reference page lacks, add it *there* first, which bumps the hash and forces the guide to be
    regenerated in the same commit — exactly the intended order.
22. `guide/START-HERE.md` has no source page. It is exempt from rules 17, 18 and 21, and is where
    cross-cutting material lives that no single reference page owns.

**Never fix a fact in `guide/`.** If the two layers disagree, the reference page is the truth and
the guide is stale: fix `docs/`, regenerate the guide, ship both in one PR. A disagreement is a bug
report against `docs/`, not an editing job in `guide/`.

**Known limitation:** a hand-edit to a guide that only rewords prose is not mechanically
detectable. Rule 21 catches invented facts; rule 18 catches a stale guide; review catches the rest.

## Updating `verified-at`

`verified-at` is the short SHA the doc was last checked against, from `git rev-parse --short HEAD`.
Bump it whenever you confirm or correct a doc. A doc whose `verified-at` is far behind `main` has
not been checked recently — treat its details as hints and confirm them in the code before relying
on them.

## Conventions & invariants

- A template is addressed by its path under `templates/` without the extension, as a
  `templates.TplName` constant in the handler — `"repo/issue/list"` is
  `templates/repo/issue/list.tmpl` (`routers-web.md`).
- **The handler's `ctx.Data` is the only data channel.** A template cannot reach anything the
  handler did not put there, and `ctx.RootData` inside a template context is that same data.
- Data destined for JavaScript goes through `ctx.PageData`, which `base/head_script.tmpl` emits as
  `window.config.pageData` — a separate channel from `ctx.Data`.
- **Every user-visible string is a locale key**, written `{{ctx.Locale.Tr "repo.issues.new"}}` or
  `ctx.Locale.TrN` for plurals. Never a literal. Keys are added only to
  `options/locale/locale_en-US.json`; the other locales come from Crowdin.
- Composition is `{{template "base/head" .}}` style includes. New shared markup goes in `shared/`,
  not copied between areas.
- `dict` is lowercase for historical reasons; new template functions get uppercase names
  (`helper.go` says so at the definition).
- Mail templates use a different, smaller function set — `mailBodyFuncMap` and
  `mailSubjectTextFuncMap` in `modules/templates/mail.go`. A helper added for pages is not
  available in `templates/mail/`.
- Class attributes are written as one readable unit including their conditionals
  (`frontend-css.md`).
- Hook frontend behaviour up declaratively with `data-global-init` / `data-global-click`
  attributes rather than inline script (`frontend-js.md`).
- `.tmpl` files are tab-indented (`.editorconfig`).

## Recipes

**Add a page's template.** Create the `.tmpl` under the matching area directory, include
`base/head` and `base/footer`, declare the `TplName` constant in the handler, and add every string
as a locale key.

**Share markup between pages.** Put the partial in `templates/shared/` and include it from both
places. Two near-identical partials in two area directories is the thing to avoid.

**Add a template function.** Add it to the map returned by `newFuncMapWebPage` in
`modules/templates/helper.go` and implement it in the matching `util_*.go`. Prefer passing prepared data from the handler — a function that
does database work at render time is a performance bug.

**See a component in isolation.** Run Gitea in development mode and open `/devtest`.

## Gotchas

- A misspelled key in `ctx.Data` renders as empty, not as an error. Check the handler when

52	  `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer; never add `Co-Authored-By` or `Signed-off-by`
53	  (`AGENTS.md`).
54	
55	## Recipes
56	
57	**Build and run.** `make build` then `./gitea web`. `make watch` rebuilds on change during
58	development.
59	
60	**The targets worth memorising.**
61	
62	```sh
63	make fmt            # format Go
64	make lint-go        # Go linters
65	make lint-js        # TypeScript linters
66	make tidy           # after go.mod changes
67	make generate-swagger  # after editing API swagger comments
68	make help           # everything else
69	```
70	
71	**Frontend only.** `pnpm install` then `pnpm exec vite build`; no Go rebuild needed for CSS or TS
72	changes if you are running `make watch`.
73	
74	**The rebuild loop.** A `.go` change needs the binary rebuilt and restarted. A `.ts` or `.css`
75	change needs the frontend assets rebuilt. A `.tmpl` or locale change is picked up on reload in
76	development. `make watch` covers all of them (`docs/development.md`).
77	
78	## Gotchas
79	
80	- `make lint-go` is slow on a cold cache. Run it once before pushing rather than on every save.
81	- A swagger comment edit that is not followed by `make generate-swagger` passes locally and fails
82	  CI.
83	- Build artifacts (`gitea`, `data/`, `custom/`, `public/assets/*`) are gitignored — check
84	  `git status` before committing (`STUDENTS.md` §7).
85	- The repository expects LF endings; a CRLF commit shows as a whole-file diff.
86	
87	## Related
88	
89	- `testing.md` — the test targets
90	- `architecture.md` — what the layers are that you are linting
91
```

6	
7	<!-- Derived from docs/build-and-tooling.md. Do not edit by hand: fix the reference doc and
8	     regenerate this file. See MAINTENANCE.md rules 16-22. -->
9	
10	# Building, linting and shipping, in plain English
11	
12	**In one sentence:** a handful of `make` commands you should run before every push, and a few rules
13	that will bounce your pull request if you do not know them in advance.
14	**Come here when:** a lint or build step failed, you are unsure what to run, or you are about to
15	open a pull request.
16	
17	## What this is
18	
19	`make` is the front door to everything: building, running, testing, linting and generating. `make
20	help` lists every target; the ones that matter day to day are below.
21	
22	## Why it exists
23	
24	**Because a project with five people needs the machine to enforce consistency, not the reviewers.**
25	
26	If formatting and import order were matters of taste, every pull request would collect comments
27	about them, and reviewers would spend their attention on whitespace instead of logic. So the tools
28	decide, `make fmt` applies their decision, and nobody argues.
29	
30	The other half is that **some things cannot be checked by reading the code**. Whether a generated
31	file is up to date, whether a new file has its licence header, whether you imported a package the
32	project has banned — those are mechanical, and CI checks them. Knowing which ones exist means you
33	find out locally in seconds rather than from a failed build twenty minutes later.
34	
35	## Words you'll meet
36	
37	- **target** — a named command in the `Makefile`, run as `make <target>`.
38	- **linter** — a tool that reports suspicious or non-conforming code.
39	- **formatter** — a tool that rewrites code into a canonical shape.
40	- **import order** — the required grouping of imports, enforced automatically.
41	- **banned import** — a package the project forbids, with a replacement.
42	- **generated file** — one produced by a tool and committed, which must never be hand-edited.
43	- **Conventional Commits** — the required `type(scope): subject` format for commit and PR titles.
44	
45	## What's in these files
46	
47	| Where | What it is for |
48	| --- | --- |
49	| `Makefile` | Every build, lint, test and generate target. |
50	| `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` | Frontend dependencies. |
51	| `vite.config.ts` | The frontend build. |
52	| `.golangci.yml` | Which Go linters run, and their configuration. |
53	| `eslint.config.ts`, `stylelint.config.ts` | TypeScript and CSS linting. |
54	| `.editorconfig` | Whitespace rules. |
55	| `tools/lint-shell.sh` | Shell script checking. |
56	| `tools/lint-go-all.go` | The copyright-header check and the Go lint passes. |
57	
58	## The rules, and why
59	
60	**Before committing, `make fmt`. Before pushing, `make lint-go` or `make lint-js`** depending on
61	what you touched.
62	
63	**After changing dependencies, `make tidy`** — and justify the change in the pull request. A
64	dependency is a long-term commitment for the whole project.
65	
66	**New Go files need a copyright header with the current year**, in an exact form the linter checks.
67	Copy the header from a neighbouring file.
68	
69	**Some imports are banned, with replacements.** The standard JSON package is banned in favour of the
70	project's own; so are a handful of others, each with a stated reason. This is not stylistic — it is
71	how the project keeps an implementation swappable and avoids known-bad packages.
72	
73	**Import order is enforced**: standard library, then this project's packages, then a blank line,
74	then everything else. `make fmt` applies it, so you never have to arrange them by hand — but if you
75	skip `make fmt`, this is often what fails.
76	
77	**A pull request that changes the UI must include "after" screenshots**, and "before" ones too
78	unless it is a new feature. Worth knowing *before* you finish the work, so you capture the "before"
79	while you still can.
80	
81	**Whitespace is checked**: no trailing spaces, LF line endings, a final newline.
82	
83	**Generated files are committed and verified.** The API specification is generated from the swagger
84	comments, and CI fails when the committed version does not match. Never hand-edit a generated file;
85	regenerate it.
86	
87	**Commit messages and PR titles use Conventional Commits**, with an `Assisted-by:` trailer, and
88	never `Co-Authored-By` or `Signed-off-by`.
89	
90	## How to actually do it
91	
92	**Build and run.** `make build`, then `./gitea web`. `make watch` rebuilds as you save and is worth
93	setting up on day one.
94	
95	**The commands worth memorising.**
96	
97	```sh
98	make fmt               # format Go — run before every commit
99	make lint-go           # Go linters
100	make lint-js           # TypeScript linters
101	make tidy              # after changing dependencies
102	make generate-swagger  # after editing API swagger comments
103	make help              # everything else
104	```
105	
106	**Know what to rebuild.** A `.go` change means rebuilding the binary and restarting it. A `.ts` or
107	`.css` change means rebuilding the frontend assets. A template or locale change is picked up on
108	reload in development. `make watch` handles all of them, which is why it is worth the setup.
109	
110	## Traps, and what they look like
111	
112	**CI fails on the swagger check and you never touched the specification.** You edited a swagger
113	comment. Run `make generate-swagger` and commit the regenerated file with your change.
114	
115	**Lint complains about your imports and you cannot see the problem.** Import order. Run `make fmt`.
116	
117	**Lint rejects an import that works fine.** It is on the banned list — the message names the
118	replacement.
119	
120	**Your new Go file fails lint immediately.** Missing or malformed copyright header. Copy it from a
121	neighbour and set the current year.
122	
123	**A reviewer asks for "before" screenshots you can no longer take.** The UI has already changed on
124	your machine. Capture them before you start.
125	
126	**`make lint-go` feels painfully slow.** It is, on a cold cache. Run it once before pushing rather
127	than after every save.
128	
129	**You commit something that should not be there.** Build artefacts — the binary, the data and custom
130	directories, the built assets — are ignored, but check `git status` before committing anyway.
131	
132	**A whole file shows as changed and you only edited one line.** Line endings. The repository expects
133	LF.
134	
135	## Where to go next
136	
137	- `docs/build-and-tooling.md` (in this folder) — the reference page this was written from
138	- `testing.md` — the test commands
139	- `architecture.md` — what the layers are that you are linting
140
```

2	source: docs/i18n.md
